name: Iteration Planning
one_liner: Capacity, goal, tasks, commitment, confidence — the iteration's first activity.
purpose: Iteration Planning creates a plan and a strategy that accounts for the team's availability and capacity to reach the agreed-upon goal. It exists because iterations are short, so a well-defined strategy is essential to keep the A-PCT focused on meaningful delivery iteration after iteration. By the end the team should hold a clear, well-defined Iteration Goal and a generated iteration Work Items List — the vital elements of the Iteration Plan.
meta: Once per iteration — the first activity conducted by the A-PCT in the iteration
Two hours for each iteration week (four hours for a two-week iteration)
A typical A-PCT of five to nine Agile Team Members
A prioritised Work Items List with acceptance criteria already defined
Iteration Goal · iteration Work Items List · Commitment Agreement · Vote of Confidence
§5.1, pp. 41–45 (RAM p. 45; Appendix B.2 p. 95, under Planning)

diagram.sec: Setup — before the ceremony (not a step, p. 45)
items: Have the Work Items List prepared: PrOw prioritises it, supported by TeCo and ArOw
Have the acceptance criteria defined for every refined and estimated item
Assess ATeM capacity in advance where possible; TeCo states the operating rules first
The organics (Fig. 5.1): prioritised WIL → PrOw proposes a goal → team weighs capacity and capability → team decides what, how and how long → is the goal achievable?
Each ATeM building the solution states how much time — preferably in hours — they can give the iteration
The exercise must consider team members' holidays, public holidays and other events
Worked example: ten calendar days with one public holiday = 9 working days
Capacity: 9 days × 7 hours = 63 hours for that Agile Team Member
Unplanned events (production bugs, support, corporate meetings) also reduce availability
Guideline: take a further allowance — e.g. 10% — off each member's calculated availability
Defining the Iteration Goal is the Product Owner's responsibility
It must start with a prioritised Work Items List
The PrOw evaluates the existing items and formulates a goal that is meaningful and adds value to the solution
The PrOw relays the goal to the rest of the A-PCT so they focus on the most relevant items
An initial agreement is not approval — the ATeMs must still confirm their availability and capacity

diagram.sec: 3. Define the Work to be Done (§5.1.2.3) — the eight-step loop
items: 1. The A-PCT picks up the first item in the WIL related to the iteration goal
2. As a team, they identify the tasks they believe are required to build and deliver that item
3. Each task is chosen by an Agile Team Member for implementation
4. The ATeM estimates the task — it should be no bigger than 12 hours
5. Each ATeM verifies availability after taking the task
6. If every ATeM still has availability, the team picks up the next Work Item from the WIL
7. If an ATeM verifies the task cannot be delivered, other team members perform a check; if no other member can do it, the team should stop progress
8. Once the team reaches full capacity, evaluate whether the iteration goal can be reached or must be adjusted — which is the next step, the Commitment Agreement
Formalises the agreement between the Product Owner and the rest of the Agile Team Members per the Iteration Goal
Critical because it aligns everyone's expectations transparently in terms of team delivery
Scenario 1 — the team confirms it can reach the Iteration Goal (the simplest case)
Scenario 2 — the team cannot reach it: it proposes a less ambitious, achievable goal and the PrOw evaluates the feedback and adjusts
Scenario 3 — the team can deliver beyond it: the PrOw confirms that the extra Work Items are indeed the most relevant ones
Each ATeM and the PrOw use a finger count from 1 to 5: 1 = no confidence at all, 5 = 100% sure we will complete it successfully
1. ATeMs and PrOw take a minute to assess their confidence
2. On the count of three, everyone raises their hand at the same time
3. The facilitator asks the 5's to lower their hands, then the 4's, and finally the 3's
4. Team members who rate 2 or 1 explain their concerns and doubts
5. The entire A-PCT then performs the required adjustments, if any, to address those concerns
Once there are no more 1's or 2's, the Vote of Confidence ends — and with it, the Iteration Planning

diagram.sec: Guidelines worth memorising (not a step, p. 45)
items: Have an extra two or three work items decomposed after the vote, in case of spare time or a dropped item
"Difficult-to-find" tasks: when the team struggles to find more tasks for an item, move to the next work item
Yesterday's weather: PM²-Agile does not recommend using past velocity to set capacity, but the PrOw may use it to sanity-check the goal

Participants: TeCo facilitates and keeps the time slot · ATeM executes and builds the iteration WIL · PrOw proposes the goal and clarifies · ArOw supports goal definition for enablement work · PM is informed

fields.what: A meaningful goal that adds value to the solution, formulated by the PrOw from the prioritised WIL, and the thing that keeps the team focused all iteration.
fields.who: PrOw proposes and is Accountable · A-PCT commits
fields.pollux: "A Risk analyst can break exposure down by instrument, traceable to the lending platform."

fields.what: The mandatory input. Because it reflects the work to implement the solution, it must always be prioritised so the PrOw can propose a relevant, aligned goal.
fields.who: PrOw R · TeCo and ArOw support the preparation
fields.pollux: Prioritised on 10 Apr at the Release Planning prioritisation session, before planning.

fields.what: How much time, preferably in hours, each ATeM can dedicate to the next iteration, after holidays, public holidays and other events.
fields.pollux: 189 hours across four builders for iteration 7.

fields.what: The guide's arithmetic: a seven-hour working day, an iteration of ten calendar days with one public holiday, so 9 days × 7 hours = 63 hours.
fields.pollux: Easter Monday, 02 Apr 2029, gives iteration 7 exactly nine working days.

fields.what: A reserve for production bugs, support and other unforeseen work: e.g. 10% taken off each member's availability after the capacity calculation.
fields.pollux: 10% held back; Lamarr's 63 hours becomes 57 planned hours.

fields.what: Members may compute individual capacity before the ceremony to save time; the TeCo must first make the operating rules clear, especially the unplanned allowance.
fields.who: TeCo sets the rules · ATeM computes
fields.pollux: Lovelace collects hours by the Friday before each planning session.

fields.what: A unit of work identified by the team for a Work Item, chosen by one ATeM, and estimated by that ATeM. It should be no bigger than 12 hours.
fields.who: Identified as a team · owned by one ATeM
fields.pollux: Babbage's 16-hour sync task was split into two 8-hour tasks.

fields.what: A task estimate should not exceed 12 hours. Anything larger is decomposed; the ceiling exists so progress is visible within a day or two.
fields.pollux: Nothing over 12 hours survives into a POLLUX iteration plan.

fields.what: After taking a task, each ATeM re-verifies remaining availability. Only if every member still has availability does the team pull the next Work Item.
fields.pollux: Eiffel hit his ceiling on WIL-124, so the team stopped adding to his queue.

fields.what: If an ATeM verifies a task cannot be delivered, other members check whether they can take it. If nobody can, the team should stop progress.
fields.pollux: Nobody but Babbage could take the sync engine work — the queue stopped there.

fields.what: The formal agreement between the PrOw and the ATeMs on the Iteration Goal, aligning everyone's expectations transparently in terms of team delivery.
fields.pollux: Signed for 29 points on 03 Apr 2029 after the goal was trimmed once.

fields.what: The team finds it cannot achieve the goal; it discusses with the PrOw and proposes a less ambitious, achievable goal, which the PrOw evaluates and adjusts.
fields.pollux: Curie dropped the maturity export from the goal rather than extend the timebox.

fields.what: The team finds it can deliver beyond the goal; the discussion confirms that the extra Work Items taken on are indeed the most relevant ones.
fields.pollux: Happened in iteration 5, when two Release 1 stories were pulled forward.

fields.what: A closing check where every ATeM and the PrOw express, by finger count, how comfortable they are with the plan just agreed.
fields.who: ATeMs and PrOw vote · TeCo facilitates
fields.pollux: Lamarr voted 2 over the batch-window collision; the plan changed.

fields.what: 1 to 5, where 1 means "no confidence at all" and 5 means "I'm 100% sure we will complete it successfully".
fields.pollux: Iteration 7 first round: Eiffel 4 · Einstein 4 · Curie 4 · Babbage 3 · Lamarr 2.

fields.what: The facilitator asks the 5's to lower their hands, then the 4's, then the 3's — so only the 2's and 1's remain visible and explain their concerns.
fields.pollux: Lovelace runs it hands-up so nobody re-votes after seeing the room.

fields.what: Adjustments are made until there are no more 1's or 2's. Only then does the Vote of Confidence — and the Iteration Planning — end.
fields.pollux: Second round after dropping WIL-131: 4 · 4 · 4 · 4 · 3.

fields.what: After full capacity is reached and the vote is finished, decompose another two or three items. They are not in the iteration, but are ready if time frees up.
fields.pollux: WIL-133 and WIL-136 decomposed and parked for iteration 7.

fields.what: When decomposing an item the team will reach a point where it struggles to find more tasks; when that happens it should move to the next work item.
fields.pollux: The drill-through story stalled at four tasks, so the team moved on.

fields.what: Using past velocity to set current capacity. PM²-Agile does not recommend it, but the PrOw may use velocity to judge how realistic the goal is.
fields.who: PrOw, as a sanity check only
fields.pollux: Curie compares the 34-point average against the 29 points committed.

fields.what: The artefact the ceremony feeds: iteration dates, the Iteration Goal, the committed Work Items, dependencies, risks and the initial burndown chart.
fields.who: TeCo R · PM A · PrOw C
fields.pollux: Iteration Plan 7 opened 03 Apr, closed after the review on 13 Apr.

fields.what: Supports and facilitates the ceremony, helps the team keep the time slot, and detects anti-patterns that could jeopardise the meeting's success.
fields.pollux: Lovelace holds the four hours and stops the goal debate reopening.

fields.what: Besides acting as an ATeM, the ArOw supports the PrOw on goal definition when enablement work is involved, clarifying dependencies and mitigating architectural risks.
fields.pollux: Einstein defends WIL-121, the sync enabler, as a precondition for everything else.

fields.what: The Project Manager is informed about the Iteration Goal and the plan the A-PCT defined to achieve it. The PM does not run or attend to direct the ceremony.
fields.pollux: You receive the goal and the 29-point commitment; you do not negotiate it.

traps: Two hours per iteration WEEK, not two hours per iteration.
The PrOw is Accountable for the goal; the ATeMs are Responsible for the ceremony.
Iteration Planning does not refine or prioritise the WIL — that is Release Planning.
12 hours is a task ceiling, not an estimating unit or a story size.
5's, 4's then 3's lower their hands; only 1's and 2's must explain.
